chapter_theme: Manimekalai feeds the crowd from the bowl a chaste wife first filled and cures Kayasandigai's insatiable 'elephant-fire' hunger; Kayasandigai tells how, as her evil deed ripened, she crushed the twelve-yearly fruit of the fasting sage Viruchikan and was cursed with hunger and the loss of her sky mantra, then sends Manimekalai to the public hall (உலக அறவி) where the hungry and the friendless sick wait, and Manimekalai, holding up Aputhiran's bowl, calls all who would receive.

cast.role: Madhavi's daughter, now carrying the Amudhasurabhi bowl
a vidyadhara woman cursed with an insatiable hunger (ஆனைத்தீ)
Kayachandigai's vidyadhara husband (called விஞ்சையன் here, not named)
an ascetic by the Pothiyil forest river who eats one fruit in twelve years and curses Kayasandigai
the earlier owner of the bowl, named in Manimekalai's call

manimekalai:17:1-16.reading: The narrator likens the bowl, whose first food a chaste wife gave, to wealth won by dharma that flows the way of the virtuous: Manimekalai gives to living beings till the receivers' hands ache and it never runs low, and Kayasandigai, who carries the elephant-fire disease in her belly, bows and asks her, as physician of life, to cure a hunger that swallows whatever is given as the sea swallowed the hills the monkeys threw when the Tall One bridged it, a hunger she says came from her old deeds.
manimekalai:17:1-16.nuance: Two causes meet in one sentence of Kayasandigai's: the hunger is a disease (நோய், 7 and 16) and the fruit of old deeds (பழ வினைப் பயத்தால், 14), so the cure she seeks is food from another's hand, not merit of her own. The epic names Vishnu's descent as Rama with the word மயங்கி (9), 'bewildered' or 'having taken on confusion', a casual Buddhist touch on a Vaishnava story that the line does not develop. She calls Manimekalai ஆர் உயிர் மருத்துவி, the Sangam title of the giver as physician of hunger turned feminine.
manimekalai:17:1-16.event: Manimekalai feeds many from the alms bowl, and Kayasandigai, bowing, begs her to cure her insatiable hunger.

claims.claim: wealth earned by dharma and spent in the way of the virtuous does not run out
present suffering is the fruit of one's own old deeds

manimekalai:17:17-32.reading: Manimekalai puts food from the bowl into Kayasandigai's hand, her burning hunger and grief leave her, and she begins her story: she lived in Kanchanapuram on the northern ridge of the vidyadharas, came south with her vidyadhara to see Pothiyil as her cruel deed was ripening, and stayed by a forest river where Viruchikan, a sage with the sacred thread, twisted matted locks and bark clothes, set a great jambu fruit like a palm fruit on a teak leaf and went to bathe in a lotus pool.
manimekalai:17:17-32.nuance: The journey itself is credited to the ripening deed (என் வெவ் வினை உருப்ப, 23) before anything wrong is done: karma here moves the traveller to the place of the offence. Viruchikan's marks (thread, matted hair, bark) are those of a Brahmin forest ascetic, not a Buddhist monk.
manimekalai:17:17-32.event: Kayasandigai, fed, tells how she came south with her vidyadhara and how the sage Viruchikan left his fruit on a leaf to bathe.

claims.claim: a ripening evil deed draws its bearer to the place where it will come to fruit

manimekalai:17:33-48.reading: Driven by her ripening evil deed she went proudly and crushed the fruit with her foot; Viruchikan, coming to eat, saw it and cursed her: the divine jambu gives one fruit in twelve years that frees a human body from hunger for twelve years, he fasts but one day in twelve years, and since she crushed his food she shall lose her sky-travelling mantra and suffer alone the elephant-fire until, twelve years on, he eats a ripe fruit here; and she tells Manimekalai that the curse of that day seems to end today, for she has destroyed it.
manimekalai:17:33-48.nuance: The curse is measured exactly against the sage's loss: he must now fast twelve more years, and she must hunger until he eats. Her own account puts the cause first in her deed (தீவினை உருத்தலின், 33) and only then in her pride (செருக்கு). Line 48 may mean the term falls today or that Manimekalai's food has ended it early.
manimekalai:17:33-48.event: Kayasandigai crushes Viruchikan's fruit, and he curses her with ceaseless hunger and the loss of her sky mantra for twelve years.

claims.claim: an evil deed, when it ripens, drives one to the very act that brings punishment
an ascetic's fast gives his word the power to lay a binding curse

manimekalai:17:49-70.reading: When the sage, himself left to wasting hunger, had gone, the vidyadhara who had fled in fear of her rash act came back grieving, told her she suffered without cause at the hands of a terrible ascetic and bade her rise into the sky, but she had forgotten the mantra; the fruits, roots and vegetables he fetched could not satisfy her, and, unable to leave her, he told her kindly of a strong city in the Tamil land of Jambudvipa where unshaken rich men help those who cannot help themselves and ascetics dwell, and bade her go there by land, so she came to this city.
manimekalai:17:49-70.nuance: Her husband calls the curse causeless (காரணம் இன்றியும், 54) where she has just named her own deed as its cause: the unit keeps both views without settling them. Puhar is introduced by its charity, ஆற்றா மாக்கட்கு ஆற்றும் துணை (64), which plays on the verb ஆற்று as Kural 225 does.
manimekalai:17:49-70.event: The vidyadhara returns, finds she has lost her sky mantra and cannot be fed, and sends her on foot to Puhar, the Tamil city of givers.

claims.claim: an ascetic's curse can fall on one who has given no cause

manimekalai:17:71-82.reading: On the day of Indra's festival the vidyadhara comes to the city, sees her hunger and pities her, counting the years to come; she bows to Manimekalai for removing her unabating hunger, says she will now go to her sky city, and tells her of the public hall in the Chakravala kottam of the stainless ascetics, with a wide gate open to all, where the hungry of every town and the sick who have no one wait, choosing their givers, and bids her go there.
manimekalai:17:71-82.nuance: The hall is described from the side of the receivers: they wait and choose who will give (இடுவோர்த் தேர்ந்து, 81), not the givers choosing whom to feed. Line 72 is unclear (see source_issues).
manimekalai:17:71-82.event: Kayasandigai thanks Manimekalai, prepares to return to her sky city, and directs her to the public hall where the hungry and friendless sick wait.

manimekalai:17:83-98.reading: When Kayasandigai has gone, Manimekalai steps aside in the high street, circles the public hall three times, enters it, worships the shrine of the old goddess whom the townsfolk praise and the pillar image that showed her the cause, and like a rain cloud over a sun-scorched bamboo forest appears with the Amudhasurabhi before the hunger-wasted, calling that this is Aputhiran's bowl and all who would receive should come, and the noise of eating rises by the hall of the rich city.
manimekalai:17:83-98.nuance: The closing ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி (97) and யாணர் (98) are the words of Purananuru 173's feast at a patron's house; here the feast has no patron, and the giver names the bowl's former owner rather than herself.
manimekalai:17:83-98.event: Manimekalai worships at the public hall and, holding up Aputhiran's bowl, calls all the hungry to come, and they eat.

links.note: The couplet says the fire-disease of hunger seldom touches one who habitually shares food (பாத்தூண்); the unit opens on a bowl first filled with a chaste wife's share (பாத்தூண், 1) and on a woman with the elephant-fire disease whose hunger came from old deeds.
links.teaches: The couplet's protection covers only the sharer's own body, while the epic shows a fire-hunger that no habit of one's own sharing could have kept off because a former deed sent it, so the cure has to come from someone else's share.

gains.a: the epic's alms bowl gains the Kural's name for hunger as a fire-disease that sharing holds off, which makes the bowl a medicine
gains.b: the couplet gains a case beyond its reach: hunger sent by karma, curable only by another's gift and not prevented by one's own

links.note: The couplet ranks the strength of those who endure hunger below that of those who remove it; Viruchikan eats once in twelve years, and when his fruit is crushed his fasting power becomes a curse of hunger on another, which Manimekalai's bowl removes.
links.teaches: The story stages the couplet's ranking and adds a reason for it: the endurer's power, once offended, can itself manufacture hunger in others, so only the giver's power ends suffering rather than moving it about.

gains.a: the epic's sage and girl gain a stated rule that ranks them, the faster below the feeder
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where the endurer's strength is not merely lesser but harmful, causing the very hunger the giver must remove

links.note: Kavunthi's penance-given curse (தவம்தரு சாபம்) turns two scorners into jackals for twelve months; Viruchikan's curse binds Kayasandigai to hunger for twelve years. Both are ascetics' curses with a fixed term, but here the cursed woman names her own ripening deed as the cause and her husband calls the curse causeless.
links.teaches: Set beside the Silappathikaram, where the curse simply answers an insult, the Manimekalai makes the ascetic's curse an instrument through which the victim's own karma ripens, and lets one voice call it unjust, so the curse is no longer self-justifying.

links.note: The goddess gives Manimekalai a mantra to travel the sky and another that cuts hunger, since the body is a lump of food; Kayasandigai has lost the mantra for going through the sky (55, and அந்தரம் செல்லும் மந்திரம் 43) and suffers a hunger no food fills.
links.teaches: The two women are drawn as mirror images: the very powers granted to Manimekalai by mantra, flight and freedom from hunger, are those the curse stripped from Kayasandigai, and Manimekalai restores the second to her by charity, not by mantra.

links.note: In the Purananuru poem the bard hears the noise of eating (ஊணொலி அரவம்) at Pannan's house and asks where the house of the physician of hunger (பசிப்பிணி மருத்துவன்) is; the epic closes with the same noise of eating (ஊண் ஒலி அரவத்து ஒலி, 97) at the public hall, after Kayasandigai has called Manimekalai physician of life (மருத்துவி, 15).
links.teaches: The epic borrows the Sangam scene of the hunger-healer's feast word for word but moves it from a patron's house, reached by a bard's praise, to a public hall with a gate open to all where anyone who will receive is called in.

gains.a: the epic scene gains a Sangam lineage: the girl with the bowl takes the old title of physician of hunger and the very sound of the patron's feast
gains.b: the poem's question of where the healer's house is, near or far, gains an answer the Sangam world lacked: a public hall that needs no patron and no praise-song

new_concepts.gloss: the chaste wife whose steadfastness gives her word power over kings, cities and nature
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 1, பத்தினிப் பெண்டிர்)

new_concepts.gloss: a curse, a word spoken in grief or anger that binds its object and comes to fruit, even in a later birth
the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (line 42, உண்ணா நோன்பினேன்)

source_issues: Line 72 (பின் வரும் யாண்டு அவன் எண்ணினன் கழியும்) does not construe cleanly: whether the vidyadhara counts the coming years and departs, or the counted years of the curse are now passing, cannot be fixed from the line; the unit is marked uncertain.
Line 48 (இந் நாள் போலும் இளங்கொடி! கெடுத்தனை!) is elliptical: it may say the curse's term falls today or that Manimekalai has ended it before its term.
